subtype: Approach: weekly burn review with a kill threshold [Revision]
passage: I share a co-working table with two founders, Reena and Jagdish, and every Friday at five they close their laptops and open a notebook. One column for what they spent that week, one for sign-ups. I have watched this for months. In March the sign-ups grew but nobody paid. Reena had written a number at the top of the page and circled it: if the runway dropped under four months and still nobody paid, they would cut. In April it did. The next Monday they cancelled the paid design tool, thanked the freelancer, and started phoning shop owners themselves, one by one, phone on speaker. I could not tell what they felt. Jagdish looked flat for a couple of days. But by Friday there was a new entry in the sign-ups column, with a small tick beside it.

qa.q: What did the founders cut when cash fell below four months?
qa.a: They cancelled the paid design tool and thanked the freelancer.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have felt after the cuts, according to the narrator?
qa.a: The narrator cannot tell for sure, but Jagdish looked flat for a couple of days, so may have felt disappointed.

qa.q: What else could the founders do besides selling personally?
qa.a: They could ask the sign-ups why nobody pays, and adjust what they offer based on the answers.

qa.q: How does the narrator see the weekly review?
qa.a: The narrator sees it as disciplined, since the limit was set in advance and the decision was not made in panic.

grounding: The founders compare spending with sign-ups each Friday and, when cash falls below the set threshold with no paying user, cut costs and sell personally.

subtype: Approach: weekly burn review with a kill threshold [Revision]
passage:
Friday, week 10. Ojas and Uday sit with laptops in a Jaipur café for their weekly review. Spent this week: design freelancer, ad credits, three paid software tools. Signups: 41. Paying users: 0. Cash left: five months. Uday writes their rule at the top of the sheet again: "Under four months of cash and zero paying users = change course."
Friday, week 14. The sheet says four months and one week. Still nobody paying. Ojas's jaw is tight. "One more ad campaign?" Uday points at the rule.
Friday, week 15. Four months, flat. They cancel two of the tools, thank the freelancer and end the contract, and stop the ads. On Monday both put on clean shirts and walk into eight coaching institutes on Tonk Road to sell the app in person. Two ask for a demo.

qa.a: "Under four months of cash and zero paying users = change course."

qa.q: What do Ojas's tight jaw and "One more ad campaign?" suggest?
qa.a: Ojas feels tense and reluctant to accept the rule, hoping a bit more spending might still rescue the old plan.

qa.q: Why was selling in person a sensible shift?
qa.a: It costs little while cash is short and brings direct talks with possible customers, like the two institutes that asked for a demo.

qa.q: How might the freelancer feel about the contract ending?
qa.a: The freelancer might be disappointed, but being thanked and told clearly makes it easier to accept.

grounding: It shows founders reviewing spending against signups every Friday and, when cash hits four months with no paying user, cutting paid tools and freelancers to sell in person.

subtype: Approach: weekly burn review with a kill threshold [Revision]
passage:
Wasim uncle stirred his tea and looked at his niece's pitch deck. "When Anjali and I started our tiffin delivery company, we were twenty-five and full of big talk. We had ten months of money. Every Friday, no matter what, we sat on the office floor with two numbers: what we spent that week, and how many customers signed up. And one rule written on the wall: if cash drops below four months and nobody is paying, we stop and change.
At month six it happened. Four months left, lots of free trials, not one paying customer. Anjali cried a little. I was angry. But we had promised the wall. We dropped the two paid delivery apps we used, let our freelance designer go, and spent the next weeks knocking on office doors ourselves with tiffins in our hands. The first paying customer was a bank branch. That rule saved us."

qa.q: What two numbers did they look at every Friday?
qa.a: What they spent that week, and how many customers signed up.

qa.q: What were Anjali and Wasim feeling when the rule was triggered?
qa.a: Anjali was upset enough to cry and Wasim was angry, but both kept their promise to the wall.

qa.q: Which choice in the story saved the company, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the Friday rule and switching to knocking on office doors, because it cut spending and put them face to face with buyers like the bank branch.

qa.q: How might the freelance designer have experienced being let go?
qa.a: The designer likely felt disappointed, but the decision came from a clear rule rather than a judgement about the designer's work.

grounding: It shows two young founders reviewing weekly spending against signups and, at four months of cash with no paying user, cutting paid tools and a freelancer to sell in person.
